strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: integrating IMU measurements into 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM to handle motion blur, low texture, and exposure variations where purely visual 3DGS SLAM degrades.

Proposes a reasonably coherent visual-inertial optimization framework that jointly minimizes visual and inertial residuals, with staged IMU initialization, per-keyframe bias estimation, loop-closure pose-graph bundle adjustment, and consistent Gaussian map updates after loop closure.

Provides extensive empirical evaluation on four datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2), including strided and extreme-condition tests, 13 baselines, and ablations for IMU fusion, loop closure, and keyframe initialization.

Demonstrates strong quantitative gains in tracking accuracy and rendering quality, often outperforming both classical VIO and recent 3DGS SLAM baselines, with additional results and implementation details in the supplementary material.
The paper is generally clear, with a helpful system overview, well-defined residuals, and reproducibility details such as dataset statistics, hyperparameters, runtime, and per-sequence metrics.
Limitations are acknowledged, including the lack of multi-camera/fisheye support and the need for high-end GPUs, which helps contextualize the contribution.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental in places: the system largely combines existing components such as a DROID-SLAM-style dense BA frontend, IMU preintegration, 3DGS mapping, and pose-graph BA, with the main new element being the addition of inertial residuals to the optimization and staged initialization.

The claimed 'tight coupling' is not fully demonstrated: the recurrent ConvGRU correspondence module appears to remain primarily visual, while IMU information mainly enters through initialization, pose propagation, and the BA objective rather than deeply influencing correspondence estimation.

Direct comparison with other visual-inertial 3DGS SLAM methods is limited. Several relevant systems (e.g., VINGS-Mono, VIGS-Fusion, GI-SLAM) are discussed but not quantitatively compared, and many 3DGS baselines are RGB-only, so some gains may stem from simply adding the IMU modality rather than from the proposed fusion design.

The real-time claim is not fully supported by the reported runtime: the supplementary material shows about 16 FPS for tracking and about 7 FPS with Gaussian mapping on an RTX 5090, with part of the IMU code in NumPy, so high-fidelity mapping is not currently real-time.

Some technical details are underexplored: the 'temporal bias smoothness term' is mentioned but not clearly formulated in the main equations, and there is no ablation isolating the effect of time-varying bias modeling or the online Jacobian-based corrections.

Evaluation is strong overall but not without caveats: MM3DGS-SLAM is not fully open-sourced for RGB+IMU, some results are copied from prior papers, and the self-captured extreme sequence uses pseudo ground truth from FAST-LIVO2, which weakens the ground-truth rigor for that experiment.
There are minor presentation and reproducibility issues, such as a likely typo in the bias residual (appearing as b_i - b_i) and a missing project-page URL, which slightly reduce polish.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing 3DGS-SLAM systems are purely visual and degrade under motion blur, low texture, exposure variation, and low frame rate; incorporating IMU sensing is a sensible and practically important direction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2) against 13 baselines, spanning indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot captures, with consistent state-of-the-art tracking accuracy (e.g., EuRoC 2.79 cm ATE vs. 4.30 for ORB-SLAM3; RPNG 1.68 vs. 3.46 for VINS-Mono).
Strong and consistently reported rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) across datasets, with the best averages in Table 3, demonstrating that robustness gains do not come at the cost of map fidelity.

Well-designed ablations isolating IMU fusion, loop closure, IMU-based keyframe initialization, and loop-closure Gaussian updates, showing each component's contribution (e.g., without IMU fusion ATE rises from 3.39 to 88.54 on strided EuRoC).

Robustness-oriented evaluation using strided frame subsampling and a self-captured extreme-condition sequence, with Recall@5/10 cm metrics that avoid the misleading low-ATE-on-short-trajectory artifact—an important and thoughtful protocol.

Clear, well-structured writing with a readable system overview figure, a clean staged IMU initialization procedure, and useful supplementary material (dataset statistics, runtime, per-sequence results).
Honest limitation section acknowledging lack of multi-camera/fisheye support and the need for a high-end GPU, plus disclosure that part of the IMU code is currently NumPy-based.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: jointly optimizing visual and inertial residuals within a bundle-adjustment-style framework is standard VIO practice (e.g., VINS-Mono, OKVIS), and the core new element is applying this formulation to a 3DGS-SLAM back end. The paper's claim that prior VIO-3DGS works use 'decoupled alternating optimization' rather than joint optimization is a fine distinction that is not fully substantiated with a direct technical or empirical contrast.

No quantitative comparison against the most directly comparable VIO-3DGS-SLAM systems (VINGS-Mono and MM3DGS-SLAM) in the main tracking tables; MM3DGS-SLAM appears only on UTMM and is partly excused by code availability. This weakens the claim of superiority over 'state of the art' for the specific visual-inertial 3DGS setting.

The 'real-time' claim in the abstract is somewhat overstated: full-system FPS is 7.09–16.40 (Table 9), below ORB-SLAM3's 22.02 and only comparable to HI-SLAM2; the enforced keyframe interval of 3 s and the NumPy implementation of IMU code both limit throughput. A clearer discussion of real-time feasibility is warranted.

The rendering comparison in Table 3 excludes MM3DGS-SLAM (the only other VIO-3DGS method) and relies on reported numbers for HI-SLAM2 in some cases, which reduces the strength of the head-to-head rendering claims.

Some design choices are stated but not fully justified or ablated—e.g., the specific thresholds for loop closure, keyframe selection, and the covariance-trace fallback for IMU preintegration drift are given but their sensitivity is not explored.

On the FAST-LIVO2 dataset, the purely RGB HI-SLAM2 baseline already achieves 10.22 cm, so the margin of improvement (6.08 cm) is meaningful but not overwhelming; a discussion of why IMU helps less in this low-frame-rate outdoor setting would strengthen the analysis.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2) covering indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot, and grayscale/RGB, with both tracking (ATE RMSE, Recall) and rendering (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) metrics.

Strong empirical tracking results: the method achieves the best or near-best average ATE on every dataset (e.g., 2.79 cm on EuRoC, 1.68 cm on RPNG, 3.24 cm on UTMM, 6.08 cm on FAST-LIVO2), and notably succeeds where all classical VIO baselines (VINS-Mono, OPEN-VINS, ORB-SLAM3) fail entirely on FAST-LIVO2.

The robustness study (strided evaluation on EuRoC and RPNG, plus an extreme-condition sequence) is a valuable addition and highlights a practical advantage over visual-only 3DGS SLAM, which degrades under frame drops and motion blur.
Ablation studies (Tables 6, 7, 18, 19) quantify the contributions of IMU fusion, loop closure, and IMU-based keyframe initialization, showing each component matters.
Supplementary material is thorough: dataset statistics, hyperparameters, runtime/FPS analysis, per-sequence rendering and tracking numbers, and per-sequence stride results are provided.
The system overview figure (Fig. 2) and the writing are generally clear and well-organized.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to a crowded field. The paper itself cites MM3DGS-SLAM, VIGS-Fusion, VINGS-Mono, GI-SLAM, and GS-LAM as VIO/3DGS SLAM systems, so the claim that 'very few' exist is overstated. The proposed system is largely a composition of existing components: a DROID-SLAM visual front-end, standard IMU pre-integration residuals, Gaussian Splatting mapping, and a pose-graph BA (which the authors state is 'inspired by [62]'). The genuinely new pieces (staged IMU initialization, joint visual-inertial optimization, and a Gaussian update after loop closure) are engineering-level refinements rather than conceptual advances.
The joint visual-inertial residual formulation (Eqs. 1–2) is essentially a standard VIO objective; presenting it as a key contribution understates the amount of prior art.

Modest gains on the dataset where vision is already reliable. On EuRoC, the improvement over the best RGB-only baseline (HI-SLAM2, 2.94 cm) is only 0.15 cm (2.79 cm). This undercuts the narrative that visual-inertial fusion is essential for accuracy and suggests the main benefit is robustness in degraded regimes rather than general accuracy.

Comparison fairness is questionable in places. Several baselines (SVO, TartanVO, DSO, MSCKF, OKVIS, VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3) are copied from other papers rather than re-tuned on the target datasets, and RGB-only methods (Splat-SLAM, HI-SLAM2, DROID-SLAM) are compared against an RGB+IMU system without always making the modality gap explicit. MM3DGS-SLAM is compared only on UTMM with copied results, and the authors note its open-source code does not fully support RGB+IMU.

Rendering improvements are marginal (~1 dB PSNR over HI-SLAM2 on RPNG and FAST-LIVO2) and the ablation for the loop-closure Gaussian update (Table 7) shows only a ~1 dB PSNR gain, raising the question of whether the mapping contribution is substantial enough for a dedicated claim.
The 'extreme conditions' evaluation (Fig. 5) is purely qualitative; no quantitative ATE/Recall is given for this self-captured sequence, weakening the robustness claim.

The 'real-time' claim is not fully substantiated. The reported FPS for tracking + GS mapping averages 16.40 on RPNG (Table 9) and is lower than HI-SLAM2 on some sequences; the supplementary admits the IMU code is implemented in NumPy rather than CUDA, and the fully optimized system is left as future work. It is unclear that the system meets real-time constraints on the hardware tested.

Some mathematical/implementation details are hand-waved, e.g., the transformation T_cb between vision and IMU frames is explicitly omitted from the equations and only mentioned as 'accounted for in the implementation', which limits reproducibility.

The comparison against VIGS-Fusion, GI-SLAM, and other recent visual-inertial 3DGS methods is missing or relegated to related-work discussion, so the claimed 'state-of-the-art' status is not fully demonstrated against the most relevant competitors.

The contribution statement is somewhat inflated relative to what is delivered; the abstract claims 'robust IMU initialization, time-varying bias modeling, and loop closure with consistent Gaussian updates' as features, but each of these is a relatively standard or incremental component.
